title: A further question: does God's wisdom forbid creating man without it, and is 'pure nature' a possible state?
source_text: XLVIII. Praeterea vero quaestio est inter Scholam Reformatam & plurimos Scholae Romanae Doctores, Annon sapientiae & bonitati divinae repugnet hominem creari absque justitia Originali; & an inter status hominis possibiles numerari debeat status ille quem Schola Romana vocat purae naturae: In quo non sit homo peccato corruptus, & tamen vera justitia careat, multaque ignorantia & infirmitate laboret, & ad malum trahatur propria concupiscentia, & appetitu adversus rationem rebellante, non secus ac res se habet in statu naturae corruptae. Quod affirmat vulgus Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, Schola vero Reformata communi consensu negat, uno forte vel altero excepto.
pass_a_gloss: But moreover there is a question between the Reformed School and very many Doctors of the Roman School, Whether it does not conflict with divine wisdom and goodness that man be created without Original justice; and whether among the possible states of man that state ought to be numbered which the Roman School calls of pure nature: In which man is not corrupted by sin, and yet lacks true justice, and labors with much ignorance and infirmity, and is drawn to evil by his own concupiscence, and appetite rebelling against reason, not otherwise than the matter stands in the state of corrupt nature. Which the common run of the Doctors of the Roman Church affirms, but the Reformed School by common consent denies, with one perhaps or another excepted.
pass_b_english: There is a further question between the Reformed school and a great many Roman teachers: whether it is not contrary to God's wisdom and goodness for man to be created without original righteousness, and whether the state the Roman school calls "pure nature" should be counted among man's possible states.

In that state man would not be corrupted by sin, yet would lack true righteousness, would struggle with much ignorance and weakness, and would be drawn toward evil by his own concupiscence and by an appetite rebelling against reason, just as things are in the state of corrupt nature. The ordinary run of Roman teachers says yes; the Reformed school, with perhaps one or two exceptions, says no by common consent.

lemmas.gloss: with perhaps one or two exceptions

choices.why: Quoted as Rome's technical term for the hypothetical state.
